title: Emergency Procedures & Evacuation
whatItIs: Every site plans for foreseeable emergencies, such as fire, flooding, toxic gas or a rescue. Everyone must know the alarm, the escape routes and where to assemble.

keyFacts.text: Arrangements for foreseeable emergencies MUST include procedures to evacuate the site or part of it.
Everyone MUST be made familiar with the arrangements, and they MUST be tested at suitable intervals.
Emergency routes MUST lead as directly as possible to a safe area, be kept clear and be signed.

keyFacts: In serious and imminent danger: stop work, report it and go to a place of safety.
When the alarm sounds, leave without delay. Don't assume it's a drill or a false alarm.
In an emergency, someone should meet and direct the emergency services at the site entrance.

items.title: Raise the alarm and leave
items.text: Use the site alarm, then leave by the signed escape route without delay.

items.title: Go to the assembly point
items.text: A place of safety where everyone can be accounted for.

items.title: Meet the emergency services
items.text: Tell them about hazards such as gas cylinders, and anyone missing.

a.label: Fire alarm test
points: Weekly, at the same time each week
People are told it's a test

b.label: Fire drill
points: The whole workforce evacuates the site
Checks people know what to do; finds bottlenecks

onTheTest.question: The fire alarm sounds while you're at a critical stage of a job. What should you do?
options: Stop and leave by the escape route at once
Wait to see if it's a drill
Phone the site office to check
onTheTest.why: HSG168: when the alarm is raised, everyone must escape without delay. Workers may be reluctant to leave at a critical stage or if they think it's a drill, which delays evacuation.

onTheTest.question: Why does a site keep a record of who is on site?
options: So everyone can be accounted for in an emergency
To decide who gets a site induction
To show the client how busy the site is
onTheTest.why: HSG151: a record of who is on site, and when they arrive and leave, helps keep track of people and helps the emergency services in a fire or accident.

traps: Emergency routes and exits must be kept clear so they can be used at any time.
Don't assume someone else has called the emergency services: the plan says who does it.
Visitors and contractors on site for only a few hours must also know the alarm and what to do.
